items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1961-01-29
items.q: And the band that I was, we were all taking lessons from the same professor, Dave Perkins.

ctx.x: Yeah, but you've been playing as a kid before then?

Well, I'd say, well, when I was going to school and I'd play like weekend jobs, you know. Maybe Friday and Saturday, Friday and Saturday and Sunday. And the band that I was, we were all taking lessons from the same professor, Dave Perkins.

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1959-01-17
items.q: That's what I took lesson on that from Dave Poick.

ctx.x: seemed like he had this all playing out, what he wanted me to play.

White Father had a violin he'd been talking to that one, and after he finally talked to this man that he had a son that wanted to learn violin, but he didn't have no big money to pay for no violin, but he wanted to get a good violin. So this white gentleman must have told him about he has a violin there, and he would sell it to read him a price. And I think my dad had bought that violin for $10, and it was a real good violin. I think that violin must have worth about $50 at that time. And, you know, I should be…
About how old were you? Can we get that?

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1979-12-05
items.q: that's where my daddy, like I said, sent me to the professor, Dave Perkins, to learn music and he decided I should learn violin.

ctx.x: How old were you when you moved?

Oh, I was almost a young boy. I remember going to kindergarten school, and I remember going to the only public school I had for blacks, out at the end of River Avenue. And when we come to New Orleans, we move on, and Boydhead and Oak, I was going to the, we could call it the, the church on the side of Cowden Avenue, it's still there, but they called it something else. That's where I made my first communion, so I must have been very young. When you first? First communion, because I'm catechic, see, and conforming…
Did you play any banjo before you went to the band?
